prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as a single prize part for Katori and Ye; my preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1. The round-1 exchange sharpened the case instead of weakening it. The invention is one concept, a magic-wavelength optical lattice that cancels the trapping light shift so that many neutral atoms can be interrogated at once. It has been reproduced and compared in several laboratories at uncertainties near 1e-18, and it is already used for relativistic geodesy, tests of varying constants and the preparation of the redefinition of the second. As an instrument builder I regard this as a capability that someone had to conceive and then push to its systematic limit, and the chain from concept to demonstration to record accuracy is unusually legible. Two names, Katori for the concept and first strontium realisation and Ye for record accuracy and many-body regimes, fit the three-person limit without forcing an arbitrary cut. I would phrase the citation around the lattice clock specifically, with no wording about optical clocks in general, so that it stays clear of the 2005 comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is the most serious objection, and I treat it as a real constraint on the citation, not a point to argue away. Credit to Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Bloom and the Paris and PTB groups is incomplete, and priority details rest on recollection and not on checked records. The redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so part of the fundamental-physics payoff is still prospective. Finally, a prize for a measurement capability can be judged less fundamental than a concept-level discovery such as topological insulators. I weigh these as reasons for careful wording and not as reasons to wait, because the demonstrated record is already strong and the two-name credit is the cleanest on the shortlist.

responses.point: The lattice clock exploits many atoms cancelling the trapping Stark shift at a magic wavelength, so it is a different concept from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, though the redefinition of the second is still pending.
responses.response: I agree with the separation and rely on it. The comb is a ruler for optical frequencies and the 2012 work controls single quantum systems; the lattice clock gives many-atom statistics with the dominant systematic cancelled by design. I disagree that the pending redefinition is a reason to wait. The BIPM process will follow the demonstrated performance, not create it, and the committee has honoured work before its largest applications arrived. I would hold the citation to the lattice clock and its magic-wavelength basis, which makes this answer to the chair's overlap question concrete.

responses.point: Topological insulators, with the Kane-Mele Z2 theory confirmed by Molenkamp's HgTe experiment, are a concept-level discovery that the lattice clock cannot match, and the 2016 prize is related but distinct.
responses.response: I accept that the Kane-Mele Z2 classification is original and that the HgTe observation was a real confirmation, and I keep B019 as my first alternative for that reason. My disagreement is about credit. The HgTe route was proposed by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and a Kane, Mele, Molenkamp trio cuts the chain between prediction and observation, while the three-dimensional work of Fu, Kane and Mele, Moore and Balents and the Bi2Se3 experiments stay outside as well. The clock case needs no comparable priority decision between theory groups. I also do not think instrument-enabling work should be ranked below concept work as a rule; I judge each by whether nature, or the technique, was changed.

responses.point: Spherical-aberration correction is a concrete invention that changed what can be measured, and broad agreement on a clean attribution does not make B048 more significant than B028.
responses.response: I agree that significance is not the same as agreement, and I do not rest on the count of supporters. My difference is in how far each invention reached into new physics. Aberration correction extended an instrument class honoured in 1986 and left an unresolved TEM versus STEM priority question around Krivanek. The lattice clock opened new measurements, including height-resolved gravitational redshift and constraints on constants. I also take your point that Lemonde, Takamoto and the ion-clock community must be acknowledged; the citation boundary is where I would put that care.

responses.point: Danielsson resisted ranking the Higgs discovery first because the three-person limit forces an arbitrary choice among Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee.
responses.response: You are right, and I have not moved the Higgs discovery back into my configuration for the same reason. Any trio from ATLAS and CMS omits leaders with equal claims, and I see no wording that avoids settling a contested question. I still hold that it is the most consequential outstanding experimental result in particle physics, but in the statute as written I will not propose a configuration whose credit I cannot defend.

responses.point: Because comb technology and ion clocks were already honoured, the citation should name the optical lattice clock with magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms, not optical clocks in general.
responses.response: I agree and would adopt that logic. The citation I propose says optical lattice clock and does not use broader wording, so it protects the prize from the 2005 and 2012 overlap. I also share your view that the demonstrated cross-laboratory comparisons already outweigh the timing argument, which is where I part with colleagues who would wait for the redefinition of the second.

uncertainties: Priority and relative contributions of Katori, Ye and other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Bloom, Paris, PTB) rest on recollection and are not verified from records.
Whether the committee will regard the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes as a real obstacle even with a lattice-clock-specific citation.
Whether the redefinition of the second, once adopted, would have changed the case for waiting; I judge that it would not, but I cannot verify the timing.
Whether a two-name credit is acceptable to colleagues who think a second prize part, such as trapped-ion quantum logic, should accompany it.
statement.conflict_note: My profile records membership in PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur and an accelerator-based particle-physics doctorate. These bear on B033 and B054, neither of which is in my final configuration or alternatives, so no recusal handling is needed for my position. I have no apparent connection to Katori, Ye or the lattice clock, to B019 or to B003 from the provided profile. No other conflict is disclosed.
